title: Go to your cell
hook: an old saying: sit in your cell and your cell will teach you everything

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was amma, mother, the desert's wise women. Your line was tend the fire.

Sit in one room with nothing to do. No phone, no TV, no book. How long before you get up? Often not long. Suddenly you need water. You remember an email. You check the fridge, though you know what's in it. There's a restlessness in us that hates staying in one place. The desert monks knew it very well, and they had a word for it and a cure. The cure was four words long, and it sounds almost too simple. Today: go to your cell.
screen: `ONE ROOM, NOTHING TO DO.` → `SUDDENLY YOU NEED WATER.` → `A FOUR-WORD CURE.`

segments.voice: A cell, for a desert monk, wasn't a prison. It was a hut or a small room, his own little space for prayer and work. Here's the story, told in the Sayings of the Desert Fathers. A brother came to Abba Moses, whom tradition remembers as a former robber turned monk, and asked for a word. The old man said, in paraphrase: go, sit in your cell, and your cell will teach you everything. No technique. No secret prayer. Just stay put. Why would that teach you everything? Because when you stop moving, everything you've been outrunning catches up with you. The boredom. The worry. The old argument you keep replaying. One desert saying compares it to stirred-up water: leave it still, and the mud settles until you can see to the bottom. Stay, instead of fleeing, the monks said, and you start to see clearly, and to notice God, who in their telling had been there the whole time. It's what Jesus said on the hillside: "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret." A closet, a cell, a small room with the door shut. Centuries later, the French Christian thinker Blaise Pascal wrote that all human unhappiness comes from one thing: we can't stay quietly in our own room. The desert would have agreed. The monks had a name for that restless itch to get up and go somewhere else: acedia. And their cure for it was never a new place. It was staying.
screen: `A CELL: A SMALL ROOM.` · `YOUR CELL WILL TEACH YOU.` · `MUD SETTLES IN STILL WATER.` · `ENTER INTO THY CLOSET.`

segments.voice: Wherever you are right now, this is your cell. Don't get up or reach for anything; when the itch comes, the sudden need to check or fix or move, name it, there's the itch, and stay. If you pray, you can simply pray to the one who is in secret.
Acedia, the monks' name for the restless itch to get up and go somewhere else. Their cure for it was never a new place; it was staying, in your small room, your cell.
Your line: stay put. As Abba Moses said, your cell will teach you everything. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Monks and nuns in many Christian traditions still keep a cell for prayer and study, and many Christians set aside a quiet room or corner where they go to pray alone.
